newsitem.title: USA: J&J enters lucrative niche with Biopsys buy.
newsitem.headline: J&J enters lucrative niche with Biopsys buy.

text.p: Johnson & Johnson's acquisition of Biopsys Medical Inc allows the company a relatively inexpensive entry to the lucrative emerging niche market for minimally invasive breast biopsies, analysts said.

Analysts deal probably would have little effect on Johnson & Johnson earnings this year, but would likely be additive to earnings beginning next year as the year-old Biopsys "Mammotome" technology begins to capture market share.
"It's a very positive move for Johnson & Johnson that will be neutral to earnings in 1997 and accretive thereafter," said Prudential Securities drug analyst Charlene Lu.

J&J said it would pay a total of $310 million in the primarily stock deal. Based on the company's estimate of a $27.55 stock price for each share of Biopsys, the deal worth $270 million, plus unspecified cash and options payments.

Lu said she thought J&J was getting a good deal price-wise, noting the company will pay only an eight percent premium over Biopsys' recent stock price. "Typically you pay a 20 percent premium for medical devices," she said.
Salomon Brothers pharmaceutical analyst Eli Kammerman said J&J was securing an early foothold in a technology destined for fast growth.
"It (Biopsys) has already been used in 58,000 procedures in a little over a year, but will be used in 300,000 to 400,000 within the next three years," he said.

Merrill Lynch drug analyst Margo Vignola noted Johnson & Johnson already had a significant market presence in minimally invasive surgery, "so this would be a nice complement and extension of their product line."
She estimated the Biopsys system was now generating about $20 million to $25 million in annual sales, making J&J's purchase price about 12 times sales.
"It's high from a price to sales basis," she said, but from a long-term standpoint "it's a smart investment."
In addition, Lu said, Biopsys' sales growth could easily accelerate with J&J's considerable market muscle behind it.
"It will have Johnson & Johnson's huge marketing power -- hundreds of sales people instead of the 12 people that Biopsys now has," she said.

Kammerman said the marriage of companies would pit J&J head-to-head against U.S. Surgical Corp which he said was the only other company with comparably sophisticated and proven technology for breast biopsies.

"It's going to be an intense marketing battle, but I think the Biopsys product will eventually get forty percent of the potential market for all breast biopsies," said Kammerman, who estimated Biopsys now held about seven to nine percent.
Lu said the Biopsys method has some advantages of being "cheaper and less invasive" than U.S. Surgical's ABBI (Advanced Breast Biopsy Instrumentation) device.

But because ABBI technology removes a bigger core of tissue, she said it is preferred by some surgeons and radiologists and has potential for use in the future for surgical removal of tumors as well as diagnosis.
Shares of Biopsys gained 1 to 26-3/4 in mid-afternoon activity. Johnson & Johnson shares eased 1/4 to 59-1/8.
